name: Accelerator Hardware Root-of-Trust
description: Integrated root-of-trust in AI accelerators with hardware-provisioned identity (e-fuse keys), secure key storage, and remote attestation capability. The accelerator can cryptographically prove its identity and configuration state to remote parties without trusting the host.

current_state.summary: NVIDIA Hopper/Blackwell have partial implementation (dependent on a CPU TEE), and Rubin extends confidential computing across CPU, GPU and NVLink while still pairing with a CPU TEE. GuardAIn (IEEE S&P 2025, formerly Ascend-CC) demonstrates an accelerator-controlled variant in research on Ascend 910A; Huawei's commercial A+K platform pairs a Kunpeng CPU TEE with an Ascend NPU TEE, i.e. the same two-TEE model. No fully SL5-compliant accelerator excluding the CPU from the TCB exists commercially.

technical_feasibility.notes: Concept proven in research (Ascend-CC) and partially in commercial products. Full SL5 requirement (accelerator-controlled, excluding CPU from TCB) not yet in production silicon.

time_to_deploy_months.notes: Chip design cycle. If vendor already has it in roadmap, faster. If not, requires influencing vendor roadmap + full design cycle.

cost.notes: R&D cost borne by chip vendor. Customer pays via chip premium. Massive if custom silicon needed.

vendor_dependency.notes: Almost entirely vendor-controlled. Customer can only influence via procurement requirements and market pressure. Must engage during architecture phase — cannot retrofit.

supply_scarcity.bottleneck: Only 3-4 entities globally can design and fab AI accelerators at frontier scale
supply_scarcity.notes: NVIDIA, Google, AMD/Intel, AWS — very few options

organizational_readiness.notes: Easy to consume once in silicon. The challenge is getting it into silicon — requires vendor cooperation.

adversary_exploitation.exploit_narrative: Without hardware root-of-trust, a compromised host system can impersonate the accelerator, load unauthorized firmware, or access weight data without detection. The accelerator cannot prove it is genuine or running authorized code.

open_questions.question: Will vendors prioritize SL5-grade root-of-trust (excluding CPU from TCB) in their roadmaps by 2027-2028?
open_questions.impact_if_resolved_negatively: Must rely on CPU TEE (weaker model) or wait additional chip generation

real_world_parallels.description: TPM (Trusted Platform Module) chips provide hardware root-of-trust for PCs — same concept extended to AI accelerators. The difference: TPMs protect general-purpose computing; this protects model weights specifically.

counters.why: Attests genuine accelerators and firmware; an enabler more than a counter
Detects modified accelerator firmware at attestation

name: Device-Controlled Memory Isolation
description: AI accelerators deny host system access to memory regions containing model weights via DMA or other mechanism. This isolation is controlled by the accelerator itself — the host cannot override it even with root/kernel privileges.

current_state.summary: NVIDIA Blackwell has partial implementation, with B200 adding native PCIe 5.0 encryption that reduces but does not eliminate the dependency on a CPU TEE controlling access. True device-controlled isolation (the accelerator denying the host independently of host software) is demonstrated in GuardAIn (IEEE S&P 2025) research but not in commercial products.

technical_feasibility.notes: Research demonstrates feasibility. Commercial implementation requires silicon changes — memory controller must be under accelerator control, not host control.

time_to_deploy_months.notes: Same chip design cycle constraint as HW-01. These are co-designed features.

cost.notes: Bundled with HW-01 — same silicon investment. Marginal cost over root-of-trust is low.

vendor_dependency.notes: Entirely vendor-controlled. Fundamental to chip memory architecture.

supply_scarcity.bottleneck: No commercially available accelerator provides true device-controlled isolation today
supply_scarcity.notes: Must wait for next-gen silicon or influence vendor roadmap

organizational_readiness.notes: Once available, adoption requires driver/framework updates but not cultural change.

adversary_exploitation.exploit_narrative: Without memory isolation, any process that achieves kernel-level access on the host (via zero-day, driver vulnerability, or BMC compromise) can directly read model weights from GPU/accelerator memory. Full host compromise = full weight access.

open_questions.question: Performance impact of device-controlled memory isolation on training throughput?
open_questions.impact_if_resolved_negatively: 5-20% training slowdown — significant at frontier scale but potentially acceptable for security

real_world_parallels.description: Intel SGX enclaves provide CPU-controlled memory isolation where even the OS cannot read enclave memory. Same principle extended from CPU to accelerator domain.

counters.why: Host root no longer reads accelerator memory holding weights
A host zero-day stops short of weights in device memory
Same, though a pool of zero-days likely includes device bugs
Closes GPU memory-leak bug classes such as LeftoverLocals

name: Accelerator Interconnect Encryption
description: Hardware-level encryption on chip-to-chip interconnects (NVLink, NeuronLink, custom fabrics) so model weights in transit between accelerators are ciphertext, not plaintext.

current_state.summary: NVIDIA Blackwell supports it and Rubin extends encryption across the NVLink domain. Google TPU (now v7/Ironwood) and AWS Trainium do not - TPUs cannot be attached to Confidential VM instances. For a lab already on NVIDIA this is a procurement decision available now; the real constraint is vendor lock-in rather than chip design cycles.

technical_feasibility.notes: Proven on Blackwell; the engineering is solved, just needs broader adoption across vendors.

time_to_deploy_months.notes: Spans two very different paths, which is why the range is wide. If the vendor already ships it, deployment is procurement: 6-12 months (NVIDIA Blackwell and Rubin support it today). If it must be added to a vendor roadmap, it is a full chip design cycle: 30-48 months. A lab already on NVIDIA reads the bottom of the range; a lab on TPUs or Trainium reads the top.

cost.notes: Cost is borne by chip vendor in R&D. Customer pays via chip price premium. Upfront = vendor investment to add feature.

vendor_dependency.notes: Almost entirely in vendor hands. Customer can only influence via procurement requirements and market pressure.

supply_scarcity.bottleneck: Only 1 of 3 major AI accelerator vendors ships interconnect encryption today
supply_scarcity.notes: Constrained by vendor roadmap decisions, not physical scarcity

organizational_readiness.notes: Once the chip exists, consuming it is straightforward. Barrier is vendor availability, not org capability.

adversary_exploitation.exploit_narrative: An adversary with physical access to the datacenter can tap interconnect cables between accelerators and passively record model weights transmitted in plaintext during training or inference.

completed_by.why: Interconnect encryption is only as trustworthy as the endpoints holding the keys. Without a hardware root of trust and verified boot, an adversary who owns the firmware owns the plaintext.

open_questions.question: Performance overhead of interconnect encryption at training scale?
open_questions.impact_if_resolved_negatively: Training throughput reduction 5-15% — significant at frontier scale but manageable

open_questions.question: Will all major accelerator vendors ship this by 2028?
open_questions.impact_if_resolved_negatively: Orgs locked to non-compliant vendors cannot achieve SL5 hardware security

real_world_parallels.description: NSA ANT catalog included FIREWALK — hardware implant disguised as RJ45 jack that passively intercepts network traffic. Same technique applies to high-bandwidth interconnects.

counters.why: Fabric taps capture ciphertext; covers accelerator links only
An in-rack interposer yields nothing readable
counters.note: Weak: accelerator fabric only; DIMM interposers and pulled drives untouched.

counters.why: Fabric traffic is ciphertext

name: Tamper Protection (Chip-Level)
description: Physical tamper protection for AI accelerator compute cores and memory where model weights exist unencrypted during computation. Detection mechanisms identify physical attacks; response mechanisms may zeroize sensitive data.

current_state.summary: Three active FIPS 140-2 Level 4 certificates remain, all IBM: the 4770-001 and 4769-001 Enterprise PKCS#11 HSMs (certs 4558 and 4553) and the 4769-001 Cryptographic Coprocessor (cert 4079). All three sunset 2026-09-21, and no module has yet been validated at FIPS 140-3 Level 4, so the count of currently-validated Level 4 modules is about to reach zero. Sixteen further Level 4 modules are already historical, so the market has contracted rather than grown. No AI accelerator has equivalent tamper protection.

technical_feasibility.notes: HSMs prove concept at small scale. Scaling tamper protection to AI accelerator chips (with massive die sizes, high power, liquid cooling) is an unsolved engineering challenge.

time_to_deploy_months.notes: Requires fundamental chip packaging innovation. Beyond normal chip design cycle — needs new materials science and manufacturing processes.

cost.notes: Massive R&D. New packaging, new fab processes, new testing. Per-chip cost increase unknown but likely significant.

vendor_dependency.notes: Completely in vendor hands. No customer can add tamper protection post-manufacture.

supply_scarcity.bottleneck: No AI accelerator with chip-level tamper protection exists. Zero supply.
supply_scarcity.notes: First-of-kind product needed. Could be 5+ years from availability.

organizational_readiness.notes: Once available, it's just buying the right chip. No org change needed to consume.

adversary_exploitation.exploit_narrative: An OC5 adversary with physical access and advanced laboratory equipment could decap chips, probe memory cells, or use focused ion beams to extract model weights during computation. Without tamper protection, the chip has no defense against physical attack.

open_questions.question: Can tamper protection scale to AI accelerator form factors (large dies, high TDP, liquid cooling)?
open_questions.impact_if_resolved_negatively: Chip-level tamper protection for AI accelerators may be infeasible — must rely on rack/room-level physical protection instead

real_world_parallels.description: IBM HSMs (FIPS 140-2 Level 4) use multiple tamper-detection layers: temperature sensors, voltage monitors, physical mesh, chemical reactive coatings. On tamper detection, all keys are zeroized instantly.

counters.why: Probing chips during physical access triggers detection or zeroisation
Seized accelerators zeroise rather than yield weights
Zeroisation denies weights from seized hardware
Probing chips triggers detection or zeroisation

name: Tamper-Evident Enclosures (Rack/Room Scale)
description: Shielded rack enclosures meeting NSA 94-106 specifications (100dB attenuation from 1kHz to 10GHz). Provide physical protection at rack or room scale when chip-level tamper protection is unavailable. Also provides EM shielding against TEMPEST attacks.

current_state.summary: NSA 94-106 shielded racks exist commercially. Used in government facilities. Not deployed in AI datacenter context. Products available from multiple vendors.

technical_feasibility.notes: Products exist meeting spec. Challenge is adapting for AI datacenter thermal requirements — shielded racks impede cooling. Liquid cooling may complicate shielding integrity.

time_to_deploy_months.notes: Procurement, installation, integration with cooling. Longer if facility wasn't designed for them (weight, power, cooling constraints).

cost.notes: Per-rack cost is high ($50-200K per shielded rack × hundreds of racks). Ongoing = maintenance of shielding integrity, cooling management.

vendor_dependency.notes: Multiple vendors produce NSA 94-106 compliant enclosures. May need customization for AI datacenter thermal profiles.

supply_scarcity.bottleneck: Shielded rack manufacturers with capacity for datacenter-scale orders + AI thermal requirements
supply_scarcity.notes: Small market suddenly needing to scale if multiple AI labs require this simultaneously

organizational_readiness.notes: Shielded racks complicate physical maintenance access and thermal management. Not a cultural barrier but an engineering one.

adversary_exploitation.exploit_narrative: Without shielded enclosures, an adversary can use TEMPEST techniques to capture electromagnetic emissions from computing hardware and reconstruct processed data. Advanced models could potentially modulate EM emissions deliberately as a covert exfiltration channel.

completed_by.why: Tamper-evident is a detection story, not a prevention one: the seal records the intrusion but only an inspection regime and an alarm response turn that record into a response.

open_questions.question: Required attenuation level for Weight Enclave racks: full NSA 94-106 or reduced spec acceptable?
open_questions.impact_if_resolved_negatively: Full spec is significantly more expensive and limits cooling options

real_world_parallels.description: TEMPEST-rated equipment has been required for classified computing since the 1960s. Van Eck phreaking (1985) demonstrated reconstruction of CRT display contents from EM emissions at distance.

reclassified.why: Hard stop for EM shielding, detection-only for tampering.

counters.why: NSA 94-106 shielding attenuates emanations by ~100 dB
counters.note: EM only: no effect on cache or timing channels.

counters.why: Enclosure seals record tampering for inspection to find
counters.note: Tamper-evident is detection, not prevention: a hard stop only for EM shielding.

counters.why: A device planted inside a sealed rack leaves evidence
Shielding blocks deliberately modulated EM channels
Shielded racks contain RF covert channels from implanted hardware
Tamper evidence shows an opened rack

name: Execution Integrity Verification
description: AI accelerators verify that code is cryptographically signed before execution — extending beyond firmware to all operator binaries and workloads. Prevents unauthorized code from running on accelerators that have access to model weights. Advanced tier (absorbs HW-10): composition-attack prevention - task-sequence attestation or verified fused kernels - so individually signed operations cannot be sequenced to leak weights. Research-stage.

current_state.summary: Firmware signing is standard on modern accelerators. Extending to workload/operator signing is not. The full SL5 requirement (all code on accelerator must be signed, no exceptions) requires new verification mechanisms.

technical_feasibility.notes: Firmware signing exists. Extending to arbitrary workloads requires either fused-kernel verification or task-sequence attestation — research-stage approaches.

time_to_deploy_months.notes: Requires both silicon features (hardware verification of workload signatures) and software ecosystem (signing all ML kernels/operators).

cost.notes: Silicon cost + building signing infrastructure + ongoing workload certification pipeline. Upper end includes the research-stage composition-attack tier (former HW-10).

vendor_dependency.notes: Needs both hardware support (verification logic in silicon) and software ecosystem cooperation (signed kernels in PyTorch/JAX/etc).

supply_scarcity.bottleneck: No complete ecosystem for signed ML workloads exists
supply_scarcity.notes: Requires building new toolchain from scratch

organizational_readiness.notes: ML researchers write custom CUDA kernels. Signed-only execution means all custom code must go through a certification pipeline — major friction.

adversary_exploitation.exploit_narrative: Without execution integrity verification, an adversary who compromises the host can load malicious code onto the accelerator — code designed to read model weights from memory and exfiltrate them. AI capability makes crafting such exploits significantly easier.

open_questions.question: Can composition attacks be prevented — where individually-signed operations are sequenced to exfiltrate data?
open_questions.impact_if_resolved_negatively: Signing individual operations is insufficient; need task-sequence verification or fused-kernel-only execution

open_questions.question: Is composition attack prevention computationally tractable for real ML workloads?
open_questions.impact_if_resolved_negatively: May be fundamentally infeasible for general workloads — must rely on restrictive allow-lists instead of general verification

open_questions.question: Does fused-kernel restriction prevent meaningful ML research?
open_questions.impact_if_resolved_negatively: Choice between security and research capability — may force all experimental work outside the enclave

real_world_parallels.description: iOS requires all code to be signed by Apple before execution on the device. This has been the single most effective defense against iPhone malware — despite billions of attack attempts.

Return-oriented programming (ROP) in CPU exploitation chains individually-authorized CPU instructions into malicious behavior. Composition attack prevention for accelerators is the hardware equivalent of defeating ROP.

counters.why: Unsigned payloads cannot run on accelerators
counters.note: Signing stops payload loading, not exploitation of signed code (ROP, living off the land).

counters.why: Unsigned payloads cannot run on accelerators
Zero-day must work inside signed code paths
Raises cost; many zero-days include signed-code bugs
Malicious kernels fail signature checks
Tampered binaries fail signature unless compromised before signing
Only signed workloads run; signed code with rogue configs still runs
Composition checks stop agents chaining permitted kernels into a dump

name: Confidential Computing / TEE
description: Trusted Execution Environments that protect model weights during computation. With confidential computing on, the hardware refuses the host OS, hypervisor and DMA access to protected accelerator memory, and attestation proves that configuration before weights are released. NVIDIA's GPU CC protects on-package HBM by access control rather than runtime memory encryption, and its trust anchor is a CPU TEE (which does encrypt the VM's own memory). It defends against a compromised host's software, not against an attacker with physical access: in 2025 a sub-$1,000 DDR5 bus interposer extracted CPU-TEE attestation keys (TEE.fail).

current_state.summary: NVIDIA H100/Blackwell have GPU TEE (CC mode) and Rubin extends confidential computing across CPU, GPU and NVLink, but all commercial paths still pair the accelerator with a CPU TEE rather than excluding the CPU from the TCB. Physical attacks are excluded from the commercial threat model, and TEE.Fail (2025) demonstrated that exclusion is load-bearing: a sub-$1,000 DDR5 memory-bus interposer defeated Intel SGX/TDX, AMD SEV-SNP and NVIDIA Confidential Computing, recovering attestation keys. Research (GuardAIn, IEEE S&P 2025, formerly Ascend-CC) shows accelerator-only TEE is possible but has not shipped commercially.

technical_feasibility.notes: Partial solutions exist commercially. Full SL5 requirement (excluding CPU from TCB, defending against physical attacks) is research-stage. Significant performance overhead currently.

time_to_deploy_months.notes: Current partial solutions deployable now. Full SL5-grade confidential computing: 2-4 years pending silicon advances.

cost.notes: Performance overhead is far smaller than once assumed, though the published measurements are inference-side: below 7% for typical LLM queries on H100 and ~3-3.5% on H100/B200, because the bottleneck there is PCIe transfer rather than GPU compute. Frontier TRAINING overhead is not established by those figures - training is throughput- and interconnect-bound rather than latency-bound - so the cost here is modelled as a marginal uplift rather than the 10-30% tax once assumed, with the training-scale figure still unmeasured in public.

vendor_dependency.notes: Entirely vendor-dependent for the hardware TEE implementation.

supply_scarcity.bottleneck: GPUs with CC mode are same SKU but feature must be enabled; full SL5-grade doesn't exist yet
supply_scarcity.notes: Current CC mode available on existing hardware. Future versions need new silicon.

organizational_readiness.notes: Requires building attestation verification infrastructure and accepting performance loss.

adversary_exploitation.exploit_narrative: Without confidential computing, any adversary who achieves host-level compromise (root/kernel access via zero-day chain) can read model weights directly from accelerator memory. A TEE closes that route against a software-only host compromise; it does not stop an attacker with physical access to the memory bus.

completed_by.why: A trusted execution environment assumes the boundary around it holds: without device-enforced memory isolation the host reads accelerator memory anyway, and without verified boot the attestation it offers is signed by whatever the adversary installed.

open_questions.question: Performance overhead at frontier TRAINING scale - inference-side measurements land at ~3-7%, but training is interconnect-bound and has no published figure. Does the inference result carry over?
open_questions.impact_if_resolved_negatively: If training overhead is materially higher than the inference measurements, the hardware uplift needed to hold frontier throughput returns as a real cost and confidential computing stops being close to free at the scale that matters most.

open_questions.question: Can CC mode defend against physical attacks? TEE.Fail (2025) answered no for current commercial implementations.
open_questions.impact_if_resolved_negatively: Resolved negatively. A sub-$1,000 DDR5 interposer broke Intel SGX/TDX, AMD SEV-SNP and NVIDIA CC, forging attestations; AMD declined to mitigate, holding physical access out of scope. Against an adversary with facility access, CC cannot be the sole protection - it must be paired with chip-level tamper protection (HW-04) and physical controls.

real_world_parallels.description: Intel SGX enabled confidential computing for CPUs since 2015. Despite being broken multiple times by side-channel attacks (Spectre, Meltdown, Plundervolt), it raised the bar significantly — attacks required months of research rather than standard exploitation.

reclassified.why: Defends against host software only; physical interposers (TEE.fail) and TEE bugs are in scope at OC4-5.

counters.why: Host root and DMA cannot read protected accelerator memory
A host-software compromise no longer yields weights in use
Same, but TEE implementations themselves have recurring vulnerabilities
counters.note: Against a large zero-day pool, TEE bugs are in scope; erodes like a probabilistic control.

counters.why: Cloud operator staff cannot read weights in use
counters.note: Weak: provider staff have physical access (TEE.fail); hypervisor-level only.

name: Verified/Measured Boot
description: All devices boot only from verified firmware/software, with measurements stored for remote attestation. Prevents rootkits, firmware-level malware, and unauthorized OS modifications from persisting across reboots.

current_state.summary: Secure Boot is available on modern servers (UEFI Secure Boot). GPU/accelerator firmware signing exists partially. Full measured boot with attestation for AI accelerators is limited to NVIDIA CC mode.

technical_feasibility.notes: Server secure boot is mature. Extending measured boot to accelerators (full boot chain attestation) is partially available and improving with each generation.

time_to_deploy_months.notes: For server-level: mostly configuration and policy. For accelerator-level: depends on vendor feature availability. For BMC/management controllers: may need firmware updates or hardware replacement.

cost.notes: Low hardware cost (features exist in silicon). Ongoing = attestation verification infrastructure, key management, boot policy management.

vendor_dependency.notes: Multiple vendors involved in full boot chain. Each must support verified boot for their component.

supply_scarcity.bottleneck: BMC/management controllers with verified boot are less common than server CPUs
supply_scarcity.notes: Weakest link is often the BMC — the component that has most privilege and least security

organizational_readiness.notes: Familiar concept to security teams. Implementation is operational, not cultural.

adversary_exploitation.exploit_narrative: Without verified boot, an adversary who achieves firmware-level access (via supply chain, BMC vulnerability, or physical access) can install persistent rootkits that survive reboots and OS reinstalls. These rootkits operate below the OS and are invisible to all software-based security.

real_world_parallels.description: Google's Titan security chip (2017) provides hardware-verified boot for all Google Cloud servers — ensuring no server boots compromised firmware even if supply chain is attacked.

counters.why: Firmware or boot implants are detected at the next measured boot
Removes cheap persistence below the OS
Modified firmware in delivered equipment fails measurement
Tampered drivers or firmware fail boot measurement
Firmware implanted during physical access fails measurement

name: Weight Encryption at Rest, Attestation-Gated Key Release
description: Weights are encrypted at rest and in transit inside the enclave with keys held in HSMs. A key is released only to an attested workload (measured boot plus TEE attestation) under a policy that names the job, the approvals and the destination. Stolen disks, stray copies and seized hardware yield ciphertext.

current_state.summary: Encryption at rest with cloud KMS keys is standard. Key release gated on hardware attestation of the consuming workload is not deployed for weights at any lab, though H100-class confidential computing and Apple's Private Cloud Compute show it can be built.

technical_feasibility.notes: Components exist (HSMs, TEE attestation); attestation-gated release at training-cluster scale is new.

time_to_deploy_months.notes: KMS-backed encryption is quick; the attestation-gated release service is the long pole.

cost.notes: HSM estate, key-release service, attestation verification and re-engineering of the training and serving data paths.

vendor_dependency.notes: Needs accelerator attestation from the vendor.

supply_scarcity.bottleneck: Engineers who have built attestation-based key release
supply_scarcity.notes: Few have done it at scale.

organizational_readiness.notes: Every job start now depends on a key service.

adversary_exploitation.exploit_narrative: Without attestation-gated release, anyone who reaches a disk, a backup or a host with the key in memory reads the weights: encryption at rest stops the thief who takes the drive, not the one who takes the server.

completed_by.why: Attestation is only as good as what it measures: without measured boot the host asking for the key can lie about its software, and without a TEE the released key sits in ordinary host memory.

open_questions.question: Can attestation-gated release scale to tens of thousands of nodes without the key service becoming the single point of failure?
open_questions.impact_if_resolved_negatively: Labs would carve out exceptions for availability, recreating plaintext copies.

real_world_parallels.description: Apple Private Cloud Compute releases data keys only to nodes whose attested software image is publicly logged.
NVIDIA H100 confidential computing mode with remote attestation became generally available.

counters.why: Every copy is ciphertext unless an attested enclave obtains the key
Protects the lab's own keys, not third-party roots (Comodo, DigiNotar)
Stolen drives or servers yield ciphertext
Seized storage yields ciphertext
Seized storage yields ciphertext if keys are destroyed
counters.note: Weak: depends on keys being destroyed before seizure.

counters.why: Storage-admin rights alone yield ciphertext
Irrecoverable-key policy removes escrow and recovery backdoors
Storage vendors and cloud staff see only ciphertext

Attestation adds a check independent of the software ACS
Hardware-gated key release survives some ACS software bugs
Split custody resists a single executive's order
A misconfigured store exposes only ciphertext
Leaked storage credentials yield ciphertext

name: Weight Custody
description: A custody register of every copy of the weights - checkpoints, backups, evaluation and serving replicas, researcher scratch copies - with approved storage locations, automatic deletion of unapproved copies, chain-of-custody records for every transfer and periodic reconciliation. RAND: limit the number of copies and where they live.

current_state.summary: Labs track checkpoints for engineering reasons, but none reports a security-grade register of every copy with reconciliation. Stray copies on research clusters, eval boxes and backup buckets are the norm, which is why RAND lists additional less-secure copies as its own attack vector.

technical_feasibility.notes: Inventory and reconciliation are ordinary engineering; the difficulty is discipline.

time_to_deploy_months.notes: Register and scanners first; deletion of unapproved copies needs research buy-in.

cost.notes: Scanning tooling, custody service, reconciliation staff.

organizational_readiness.notes: Researchers copy checkpoints to wherever the compute is.

adversary_exploitation.exploit_narrative: Without custody, the attacker skips the hardened copy and takes the one on a research cluster, an eval box or a backup bucket nobody remembers.

completed_by.why: A register tells you where the copies are; only encryption with controlled key release makes the copy you missed useless.

real_world_parallels.description: Meta's LLaMA weights, released to approved researchers only, appeared on a public torrent within a week.

counters.why: Inventory, centralisation, encrypted backups and media destruction remove stray copies
Media and RMA destruction close the waste-disposal route
No weight-bearing drives go back to vendors
Inventory sweeps find copies in misconfigured stores
Copy inventory flags new weight copies an agent creates
Fewer, inventoried copies within an insider's reach
Destroyed media and no stray drives to read

name: Access-Control Assurance & Formal Verification
description: Independent assurance of the access-control system itself: formal verification of its key components (key-release service, separation kernel or hypervisor, authorisation policy engine), protocol and cryptography review, and continuous red-teaming and code audit of the access stack (RAND SL5 formal verification of key components).

current_state.summary: Formally verified kernels exist and are fielded in defence (seL4); no lab's weight-access stack is verified or independently assured.

technical_feasibility.notes: Verified kernels exist; verifying a whole access stack is research-grade engineering.

time_to_deploy_months.notes: Proof engineering is slow and the stack must stay small enough to verify.

cost.notes: Proof engineers, audit firms, redesign of the access stack to be verifiable.

organizational_readiness.notes: Verifiable means small and unchanging, which research infra is not.

adversary_exploitation.exploit_narrative: Without assurance of the access-control system itself, the attacker skips the people and the keys and exploits the software that decides who gets them.

completed_by.why: Assurance needs an access-control system worth assuring: verifying a stack that still has long-lived credentials and keys released to any host proves the wrong thing.

real_world_parallels.description: DARPA HACMS: a seL4-based mission computer resisted red teams given root on a partition.

counters.why: Formally verified cryptographic and authentication protocols (RAND SL5)
Verified, minimal access-control code leaves few implementation bugs
Independent verification can expose planted weaknesses in implementations

name: Hardened Weight-Access & Serving Interface
description: The only paths to the weights are narrow, purpose-built interfaces: a minimal serving stack on dedicated hardware for external interfaces, no general-purpose shell on weight-holding nodes, and an ML-specific boundary that performs inference without exporting parameters (RAND SL3 permitted interfaces, SL4 specialised hardware for external interfaces, SL5 ML-specific HSM).

current_state.summary: Serving runs general-purpose inference servers on hosts that hold full weights in accelerator memory; dedicated interface hardware and ML-specific HSMs are not deployed.

technical_feasibility.notes: Narrow interfaces are buildable; an ML-specific HSM is research-grade.

time_to_deploy_months.notes: Re-architecting serving and research access around a narrow interface.

cost.notes: Dedicated interface hardware, serving re-architecture, interface assurance.

organizational_readiness.notes: Researchers want shells on the machines with weights.

adversary_exploitation.exploit_narrative: Without a hardened interface, a bug in a GPU driver, an inference server or a debug endpoint on a weight-holding host is a direct read of the weights.

completed_by.why: A narrow interface on a host the attacker can still reach around - no enclave, no memory protection - is a front door on a building with no walls.

counters.why: Minimal, memory-safe serving code behind a narrow interface; fuzzed drivers
A narrow interface limits what injected code can request
Escalated accounts still see weights only through the interface
Staff touch weights only through interfaces that prevent copying (RAND SL3)
Agents reach weights only through a narrow interface
